sentences.text: A mastodon left a trace in northern Greenland.
Not a bone.
Not a tusk.
DNA.
Broken pieces of genetic material, recovered from sediment roughly two million years old.
Look at that place today: a polar desert.
Now try to fit an elephant-like animal into the picture.
Something is missing.
Not just the animal.
The world around it.
In 2022, scientists reported evidence of a mastodon lineage from Greenland's Kap Copenhagen Formation.
Plant remains had already hinted at a greener past.
But the dirt held another way into that vanished landscape.
And the giant was only the beginning.
Because finding a trace is one thing.
Working out what left it, how it survived, and what sort of world it belonged to is a very different puzzle.

sentences.text: An animal does not have to die in front of you to leave evidence.
Living things shed biological material.
After death, more breaks down.
Water can carry some of it away, mixing it with material from plants and other animals before it settles into sediment.
Think of it as a delivery system with the address labels torn off.
That is environmental DNA: genetic traces collected from the surroundings, rather than from one intact body.
But delivery creates a problem.
A river can bring material from somewhere else.
A deposit can gather it over time.
So this is not one frozen instant.
And roughly two million years is the age inferred for the deposits, not a date stamped onto each molecule.
Before the pieces can reveal a world, they first have to survive one.
